# Isaiah 63: Verse-by-Verse Research Notes

**Gaps in this research:** I read Enduring Word, Bible.org (Utley), the Calvin page on CCEL, and the Bible Hub and StudyLight verse pages for vv. 1, 2, 3, 9, 16 and 17. For the other verses I only have Guzik and Utley. I found nothing from wesley.nnu.edu, seedbed, any Pentecostal site, any Lutheran site, catholic.com or oca.org. So there is no Orthodox reading here, and no material on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching on this chapter. Verse 18 has no comment, so it is left out.

---

**v. 1**
- **Traditional reading (Guzik):** This is the day of the LORD's vengeance. He comes "from Edom" because He judged there first and is now coming to Israel. Bozrah was Edom's capital, and its name means "grape-gathering." His answer, "mighty to save," shows that even in judgment He wants people to know He saves, not only judges. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/
- **Edom as a symbol:** Edom stands for every enemy of God's people (Benson, Poole), and in later Jewish use Edom came to mean Rome (Ellicott). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/63-1.htm. Clarke notes that "Edom" means red and "Bozrah" means vintage. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/63-1.html
- **Who is speaking?** The Pulpit Commentary says the answer plainly shows the figure is Jehovah. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/63-1.htm. Jewish writers, as reported by Gill, applied the verse to the Messiah coming from "Edom" (Rome). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/63-1.html
- **Dispensational/end-times view:** Precept Austin, citing Fruchtenbaum and MacArthur, reads this as the Messiah returning at the Second Coming by way of Bozrah, before reaching Jerusalem. https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_631-6_commentary
- **Disagreement among Protestants:** Spurgeon (Baptist) takes it as referring to "our blessed Lord Jesus Christ." Calvin (Reformed) says Christians have "violently distorted" the chapter. In his view the prophet speaks simply of God, not of Christ red with His own blood from the cross. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/63-1.html
- **Modern scholarship:** The Pulpit Commentary, quoting Cheyne, calls vv. 1–6 a separate poem that seems placed here "by accident." Ellicott treats it as a separate section but rejects a different author. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/63-1.htm

**v. 2**
- **Traditional reading:** The question shows the red is a stain, not the colour of the robe itself. "Red" (*'adom*) echoes "Edom," and the winepress may be suggested by Bozrah sounding like the word for vintage (Cambridge Bible). The Pulpit Commentary notes that grape-treaders' clothes were often splashed. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/63-2.htm
- **Does it picture Christ's sufferings?** Maclaren says no: the passage shows a judgment that crushes Messiah's enemies, and "It is He who crushes, not He who is crushed." https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/maclaren_alexander/expositions-of-holy-scripture/isaiah/the-winepress-and-its-treader.cfm
- **Catholic reading:** Cyprian (Epistle 62) reads the red garments as the Lord's Passion. Just as wine needs trodden grapes, we could not drink Christ's blood unless He were first trampled and pressed. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/050662.htm. The Catholic Encyclopedia says the red tint of the papal Golden Rose recalls His Passion, quoting this verse. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/06629a.htm

**v. 3**
- **Traditional reading (Guzik):** This judgment belongs to Christ alone. He alone atoned for sin and He alone judges. Guzik links the verse to Revelation 19:13–15. He also cites Spurgeon: believers' troubles are a Father's discipline, not punishment, because Christ trod the winepress alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/
- **Calvin (Reformed):** It is "absurd" to apply this to Christ redeeming us alone. It means God will punish Edom without needing human help. God also shows His love for the Jews by being willing to be stained with enemies' blood for their sake. A footnote by the editor (quoting Alexander) records Vitringa's view that the popular use of the phrase for Christ's sufferings led to the "forced" reading by the Church Fathers. Such an application may be used, but it is not the passage's first meaning. https://ccel.org/study/Isaiah_63:3
- **Utley:** The same winepress picture appears in Lamentations 1:15, Joel 3:13 and Revelation 14 and 19. It portrays God or Messiah as the Divine Warrior. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-63

**v. 4**
- **Guzik:** God does not love punishing sinners, but He loves vindicating His redeemed. Note the contrast: a "day" of vengeance but a "year" of redemption. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/
- **Utley:** The day of vengeance has to come before the year of redemption. They are two sides of one coming. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-63
- **Delitzsch (Lutheran):** The passage can serve as a Passion Week reading only in a limited sense. The Jehovah seen here became man in Christ, and behind His first coming stands the final coming to judgment. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/isaiah-63.html

**v. 5**
- **Utley:** God could rely on no human help; He alone could bring salvation. Utley suggests John may echo this in Revelation 5, where only the Lamb is worthy. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-63
- **Guzik:** He takes "My own arm" as stressing that Christ acts alone. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/

**v. 6**
- **Utley:** He finds three pictures of the Divine Warrior here: trampling, making drunk (judgment pictured as drunkenness, as in Isaiah 51:22–23), and pouring out their lifeblood on the ground. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-63

**v. 7**
- **Guzik:** This is an exile's prayer, and it begins with praise before it asks for help. "Lovingkindnesses" translates *hesed*, God's covenant-faithful love. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/
- **Keil & Delitzsch:** They report the critical scholars Hitzig and Knobel, who tie this praise to Edom's overthrow in vv. 1–6. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kdo/isaiah-63.html

**v. 8**
- **Guzik (quoting Bultema):** The Hebrew word for "lie" was used of a dry spring or a fruitless tree. God means His people will not disappoint Him. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/
- **Utley:** "My people" is covenant language. The verse is the reverse of Isaiah 1:2–3. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-63

**v. 9**
- **"He too was afflicted":** Guzik takes this as God suffering with His people, which he argues makes antisemitism especially wicked. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/
- **A Hebrew text question:** The written Hebrew has "not"; the scribes' marginal reading has "to him." Barnes says both make sense and the right one cannot now be settled. The Septuagint reads: no envoy or angel, but He Himself saved them. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/63-9.htm. Ellicott gives the written reading's sense: the suffering was nothing compared with God's salvation. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/63-9.htm
- **Who is the "Angel of His Presence"?**
  - Poole, Gill and Guzik say it is Christ. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/63-9.htm and https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/
  - Calvin, as reported by Guzik, saw only a serving angel. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/
  - Jewish interpreter Rashi (Jarchi) said Michael; Knobel said the pillar of cloud and fire. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/63-9.htm
- **NET Bible note:** The figure may be the "angel of God" of Exodus 14:19. In this chapter it may be equated with God's Holy Spirit. https://classic.net.bible.org/verse.php/verse.php?book=Isa&chapter=63&verse=9
- **Pulpit Commentary:** The "redemption" here is from Egypt, not the spiritual redemption reserved for the Messiah's time. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/63-9.htm

**v. 10**
- **Guzik:** Father, Son (the Angel) and Holy Spirit all appear in vv. 8–10, which he and Grogan see as Trinitarian overtones. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/
- **Utley:** "Grieved His Holy Spirit" shows the Spirit is a person. He compares Acts 7:51 and sees three divine Persons in vv. 9–10. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-63

**vv. 11–14**
- **Guzik:** In exile the one praying remembers the Exodus. "Like a horse in the wilderness" means open country: quick progress with nothing in the way. Clarke says the sea-bed was as easy for Israel as open desert is for a horse. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/
- **Utley:** He lists God's Exodus acts in these verses (the sea crossing, the Spirit among them, the arm at Moses' right hand, rest). All were done "to make for Yourself a glorious name," part of God revealing Himself to the world. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-63

**v. 15**
- **Utley:** "Look… see" are two urgent commands. The verse pictures Jerusalem pleading for God to come back to her. https://bible.org/seriespage/isaiah-63
- **Guzik:** When God's zeal feels far away, we should cry out to Him, as this prayer does. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/

**v. 16** (traditions differ on what "Abraham does not know us" means)
- **Calvin (Reformed):** He rejects Jerome's view that Abraham disowns a degenerate people. The point is that even if earthly fathers disowned them, God stays their Father. He adds that the verse does not prove the saints in heaven have no care for us. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/63-16.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** The patriarchs are dead and know nothing of their descendants, so the verse turns Israel from trusting in them to God alone. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/63-16.html
- **Ellicott (Anglican):** This looks ahead to the New Testament idea that God's fatherhood does not depend on descent. He also suggests Abraham may have been thought of as watching over his people (compare Luke 16:22). https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/63-16.htm
- **Keil & Delitzsch (Lutheran):** "Our Father" here does not yet carry the full New Testament meaning. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/63-16.htm
- **Haydock (Catholic):** Abraham would not own degenerate children, and he is not able to save them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/63-16.html

**v. 17** (the main place where traditions differ)
- **Calvin (Reformed):** God hardens by handing people over to Satan, the agent of His wrath. He rejects the explanation that God hardens only by withdrawing His Spirit. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/63-17.html. Barnes adds that in Calvin's view the godly who pray this way are not making God the author of sin. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/cjb/isaiah/63-17.html
- **Gill (Baptist):** These are the godly lamenting that their Father let them stray by holding back His grace. They are not blaming Him. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/63-17.htm
- **Adam Clarke:** "Made us err" is "a mere Hebraism" for "allowed us to err," like "lead us not into temptation." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/63-17.html. (The page does not label Clarke's tradition.)
- **Delitzsch (Lutheran, via the Pulpit Commentary):** When people scornfully reject grace, God withdraws it as a judgment and leaves their hearts unable to believe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/63-17.htm
- **Constable (dispensational):** God is not the direct cause of sin. The hardening is a judgment that lets the sin people chose rule over them. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/isaiah/63-17.html
- **Ellicott:** The prayer flees to the "election of grace" (God's gracious choice), which stays faithful when people are not. https://biblehub.com/isaiah/63-17.htm
- **Guzik on "Return":** Grogan suggests it may mean the return of God's glory to the temple. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/

**v. 19**
- **Guzik:** The one praying is not accurate in all his theology, but he expresses the pain of the human heart well. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-63/
- **NIV footnote:** NIV's main text reads "We are yours from of old," with "like those you have never ruled" as the alternative. https://ccel.org/study/Isaiah_63:3
